snapshot.title: UPSC History: Quit India Movement & INA
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC History Hook: 1942: Quit India. Do or Die: Gandhi. Usha Mehta: Radio. Satara: Parallel Gov. Bose: INA/Jai Hind. 1946: RIN Mutiny.

quick_notes.title: Quit India (August 1942)
quick_notes.detail: "Wardha Resolution". Launched at Gowalia Tank, Bombay. Slogan : "Do or Die" (Karo ya Maro). Most leaders arrested on the first day (Operation Zero Hour).
quick_notes.explanation: The Quit India movement was a major campaign launched by the Indian National Congress in August 1942, demanding that the British leave India immediately. It was based on the Wardha Resolution, which was a decision taken earlier in July 1942 at Wardha, Maharashtra, calling for mass nonviolent struggle. The movement was officially started at Gowalia Tank, a public ground in Bombay (now Mumbai), where Mahatma Gandhi gave the famous slogan "Do or Die", which in Hindi is "Karo ya Maro". On the very first day, the British government launched Operation Zero Hour, a code name for the mass arrest of all major Congress leaders, including Gandhi, to crush the movement quickly. As a result, most leaders were arrested before they could lead the protests, but the people continued the struggle on their own.

quick_notes.title: Spontaneous Uprising
quick_notes.detail: Leaderless movement. Massive strikes, sabotage of rail lines, and telegraphs. Underground Radio : Started by Usha Mehta in Bombay.
quick_notes.explanation: Spontaneous Uprising refers to a sudden revolt that happens without any single leader directing it. During India's freedom struggle, this occurred when people reacted to the arrest of major leaders by launching massive strikes, damaging railway lines, and cutting telegraph wires to disrupt British communication. An Underground Radio is a secret broadcasting station that operates without government permission. This radio was started by Usha Mehta in Bombay, now called Mumbai, to share news and encourage the movement when newspapers were banned. This radio helped spread information and keep the resistance alive.

quick_notes.title: Parallel Governments
quick_notes.detail: Nationalist govts formed in: 1. Ballia (Chittu Pandey). 2. Tamluk (Jatiya Sarkar). 3. Satara (Prati Sarkar - longest running).
quick_notes.explanation: During the Indian freedom struggle, when British rule was weakened or absent in certain areas, local Indian leaders set up their own temporary governments to run daily life and oppose the British. These were called parallel governments because they functioned alongside or instead of the official British administration. The first such government was formed in Ballia, in present-day Uttar Pradesh, in August 1942 under the leadership of Chittu Pandey, and it lasted only a few days before the British regained control. Another was the Jatiya Sarkar, or People's Government, set up in Tamluk, in present-day West Bengal, which ran from 1942 to 1944 and even operated its own courts and police. The longest-running parallel government was the Prati Sarkar, meaning Alternative Government, in the Satara district of present-day Maharashtra, which lasted from 1943 to 1945 and was led by leaders like Nana Patil; it collected taxes, settled disputes, and organized guerrilla resistance against the British. These governments showed how Indians could manage their own affairs and kept the spirit of rebellion alive even when the main Quit India Movement leaders were arrested.

quick_notes.title: Subhas Chandra Bose & INA
quick_notes.detail: Left INC (Tripuri Crisis 1939), formed Forward Bloc. Escaped to Germany/Japan. Took over Azad Hind Fauj (founded by Mohan Singh/Rash Behari Bose). Slogan : "Jai Hind", "Delhi Chalo".
quick_notes.explanation: Subhas Chandra Bose was a leader in the Indian National Congress (INC), the main political party fighting for India's freedom from British rule. In 1939, during the Tripuri Crisis, a disagreement within the INC, Bose was forced to resign as its president, so he left the party and formed his own group called the Forward Bloc. To continue his fight against the British, Bose escaped from India first to Germany and later to Japan, where he sought support from countries that were enemies of Britain. In Japan,

quick_notes.title: Impact of INA
quick_notes.detail: INA Trials at Red Fort (1945) created a massive wave of sympathy. INC leaders (Nehru, Bhulabhai Desai) defended them. Led to the Royal Indian Navy (RIN) Revolt in 1946.
quick_notes.explanation: The Indian National Army (INA) was a force of Indian soldiers who fought alongside Japan during World War Two to free India from British rule. After the war ended, the British held trials of INA officers at the Red Fort in Delhi in 1945, which means they were put on trial as criminals. These trials created a huge wave of sympathy among ordinary Indians, who saw the INA soldiers as patriots. Leaders of the Indian National Congress (INC), including Jawaharlal Nehru and Bhulabhai Desai, acted as defense lawyers for the accused INA soldiers. The anger and support generated by the trials directly led to the Royal Indian Navy (RIN) Revolt in 1946, where Indian sailors in the British navy mutinied in protest against British rule.

topic_title: UPSC History: Quit India Movement & INA
lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Final Blow'. The Quit India Movement (1942) was the most violent and spontaneous mass uprising since 1857. With the slogan 'Do or Die', Gandhi gave a clarion call for the British to leave immediately. Simultaneously, Subhas Chandra Bose led the Indian National Army (INA) from outside. For UPSC, focus on the 'Underground activities' of leaders like Usha Mehta and the significance of the 'Parallel Governments'. This is the endgame of the Raj.
